bullets.text: Machine Learning (ML) is a subfield of AI, building systems that learn from data and improve over time.
Core idea: systems learn patterns and make decisions with minimal human intervention.
Crucial part of modern technology with diverse applications.
Used in image recognition, natural language processing, predictive analytics, and autonomous vehicles.
Growth driven by large datasets, improved computational power, and advanced algorithms.
Broadly classified into Supervised, Unsupervised, and Reinforcement Learning.
Supervised Learning uses labeled data to learn input-output mappings for tasks like regression (continuous output) and classification (categorical output).
Unsupervised Learning finds hidden patterns or structures in unlabeled data, using techniques like clustering and dimensionality reduction.
Reinforcement Learning involves an agent learning to make decisions by interacting with its environment to maximize cumulative rewards.
RL is applied in areas such as robotics, gaming, and autonomous systems.
Model Training: Feeding data to a model to learn patterns and adjust internal parameters.
Features and Labels: Input variables (features) and target outputs (labels) in supervised learning.
Training and Testing Sets: Data split to train the model and evaluate its performance on unseen data.
Overfitting: Model learns training data too well, including noise, leading to poor generalization.
Underfitting: Model is too simple and fails to capture important patterns in the data.
Linear Regression: Models linear relationships for continuous output prediction.
Logistic Regression: Used for classification, predicting the probability of class membership.
Decision Trees: Non-linear model that splits data based on feature values, easy to interpret.
Random Forest: Ensemble method combining multiple decision trees to improve prediction performance.
Support Vector Machines (SVM): Finds an optimal hyperplane to separate data points for classification.
Neural Networks: Brain-inspired models capable of learning complex patterns, used in deep learning.
Healthcare: Disease diagnosis, drug discovery, and personalized treatment recommendations.
Finance: Fraud detection, credit scoring, and algorithmic trading.
Marketing: Customer segmentation, personalized recommendations, and targeted advertising.
Autonomous Vehicles: Processing sensor data, decision-making, and safe navigation.
Natural Language Processing (NLP): Language translation, sentiment analysis, and text summarization.
Training and Testing: Models are evaluated using separate datasets to assess performance.
Classification Metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score are commonly used.
Regression Metrics: Mean squared error (MSE) or R-squared are used for continuous predictions.
Cross-Validation: Technique to ensure models generalize well to unseen data by splitting into multiple subsets.
Hyperparameter Tuning: Optimizing model settings (hyperparameters) using methods like grid or random search.
Data Quality and Quantity: Requires large amounts of accurate, consistent, and complete data; labeled data collection can be difficult.
Interpretability: Many complex models are difficult to understand, posing issues in high-stakes applications.
Bias in Data: Models can inherit biases from training data, leading to unfair or unethical outcomes.
Overfitting and Underfitting: Common issues where models either learn noise or are too simple to capture patterns.
Continuous Evolution: Advancements in deep learning, reinforcement learning, and explainable AI (XAI).
Increased Role: Growing computational power and datasets will expand ML's significance across industries.
Integration: ML applications will become more integrated into daily life, enabling smarter technologies.
Ethical Considerations: Responsible AI practices will be essential as the field progresses.
